Direct object pronouns

mitilolacivilile
meyouhim, ither, itusyou (pl.)them (m.)them (f.)

Unlike English, they go before the conjugated verb, or attach to the end of an infinitive.

Il pane? Lo compro io.The bread? I'll buy it.
Voglio vederlo. = Lo voglio vedere.I want to see him (it). Both word orders are correct.

In the passato prossimo, the participle agrees with lo, la, li, le: “Giulia? L'ho vista ieri.” “I biglietti? Li ho comprati.”

", "

Indirect pronouns and piacere

mitiglilecivigli
to meto youto himto herto usto you (pl.)to them

Just like English “to him” / “to her”, Italian makes the distinction: gli telefono (I call him), le telefono (I call her). Note that telefonare takes an indirect object (telefonare a), while English “call” takes a direct one.

Formal address: La as a direct object, Le as an indirect one. “Signora, La ringrazio.” “Signore, Le telefono domani.”

Piacere

It works like “to be pleasing to”: the verb agrees with the thing that is liked, and the person who likes it is an indirect pronoun.

Mi piace il gelato. Mi piacciono gli spaghetti.I like ice cream. I like spaghetti. (literally: ice cream is pleasing to me, spaghetti are pleasing to me)
", "

Ci and ne

English has no exact equivalent. Ci replaces a place (“there”); ne replaces a quantity (“of it, of them”), which English often leaves unsaid. In Italian, you can't leave them out.

Vai a Roma? — Sì, ci vado domani.Are you going to Rome? Yes, I'm going (there) tomorrow.
Quanti caffè bevi? — Ne bevo tre.How many coffees do you drink? I drink three (of them).

With ne in the passato prossimo, the participle agrees with the quantity: “Quante mele hai comprato? — Ne ho comprate quattro.”

“There is one (of them)” is ce n'è uno / ce n'è una.
